name: E18-D80NK adjustable IR proximity switch
description: Diffuse-reflective infrared proximity switch in an 18 mm threaded barrel: it sends modulated IR (so ordinary room light and sunlight barely disturb it) and switches its output when something is within the range set by the rear potentiometer, about 3-80 cm (white objects are seen furthest, black closest). Gives on/off only, not a distance. NPN open-collector output, normally open: OUT is pulled LOW when an object is detected and needs a pull-up resistor otherwise. Runs on 5 V DC, 10-15 mA. Sold as: E18-D80NK-N adjustable infrared proximity switch (orange 18 mm x 45 mm body, 20 cm 3-wire lead with DuPont plug: red VCC, black GND, yellow OUT), also sold as plain E18-D80NK.
eli5: A little tube that shines invisible light and tells your board when something comes close, up to almost a metre away, like an automatic door sensor.

pins.name: VCC
pins.description: Supply, 5 V DC (red wire on the E18-D80NK-N; brown on some older batches). Wire it to the board's 5V/VBUS pin.

pins.name: GND
pins.description: Ground (black wire on the E18-D80NK-N; blue on some older batches).

pins.name: OUT
pins.description: NPN open-collector output (yellow wire on the E18-D80NK-N; black on some older batches): pulled LOW while an object is detected, otherwise open. Needs a pull-up to the microcontroller's 3.3 V logic (the GPIO's internal pull-up, or 1-10 kOhm to 3V3). Sinks up to 100 mA.

buildNotes: It is a sensor on a lead, not a breadboard module: the three wires end in a DuPont plug (or bare ends). Wire colours differ between batches, so go by the label or the seller's sheet: E18-D80NK-N is red = VCC, black = GND, yellow = OUT; older E18-D80NK lots are often brown = VCC, blue = GND, black = OUT. Swapping supply and ground can destroy the sensor.
Power it from 5 V (the board's 5V / VBUS pin), not 3V3: the datasheet specifies 5 V DC.

OUT is an NPN open-collector switch, active LOW: it reads 0 when something is in range. The datasheet asks for a pull-up on OUT; pull it up to 3V3 (the GPIO's internal pull-up, or 1-10 kOhm to 3V3), never to 5 V on an ESP32 or Pico.

Some sellers' units have their own pull-up inside to VCC. Before connecting OUT to a 3.3 V board, power the sensor and measure OUT to GND with nothing in front: if it reads about 5 V, put a 10 kOhm / 20 kOhm divider between OUT and the GPIO.
Set the range with the potentiometer on the back (a small screwdriver): the red LED on the back lights while it detects. Dark matte objects are seen much closer than white ones.
There are also 6-36 V versions sold under the same name: their output can rise to the supply voltage, so check the label before wiring.

example.code:
from e18d80nk import E18D80NK
import time

sensor = E18D80NK({OUT})
while True:
    print('Object: %s' % ('YES' if sensor.detected() else 'no'))
    time.sleep(0.5)

test.title: Reports an object when the sensor is triggered
